claim: The lumen of the small intestine is filled with particulates including microbes, therapeutic particles, and food granules.
source: The lumen of the small intestine (SI) is filled with particulates: microbes, therapeutic particles, and food granules.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published literature about the types of particles found in the small intestine.

claim: Particles spontaneously aggregate in SI luminal fluid ex vivo.
source: Here, we demonstrate that particles spontaneously aggregate in SI luminal fluid ex vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing aggregation in ex vivo assays.

claim: Mucins and immunoglobulins are not required for aggregation of PEG-coated particles in SI luminal fluid.
source: We find that mucins and immunoglobulins are not required for aggregation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from MUC2KO and Rag1KO mice showing aggregation still occurs in the absence of these molecules.

claim: Aggregation can be controlled using polymers from dietary fiber in a manner qualitatively consistent with polymer-induced depletion interactions.
source: Instead, aggregation can be controlled using polymers from dietary fiber in a manner that is qualitatively consistent with polymer-induced depletion interactions, which do not require specific chemical interactions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing aggregation behavior with different dietary fibers and theoretical modeling of depletion interactions.

claim: Aggregation is tunable by feeding mice dietary fibers of different molecular weights.
source: Furthermore, we find that aggregation is tunable; by feeding mice dietary fibers of different molecular weights, we can control aggregation in SI luminal fluid.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing aggregation in mice fed pectin versus Fibersol-2.

claim: The molecular weight and concentration of dietary polymers play an underappreciated role in shaping the physicochemical environment of the gut.
source: This work suggests that the molecular weight and concentration of dietary polymers play an underappreciated role in shaping the physicochemical environment of the gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and theoretical analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: PEG-coated particles have little or no chemical interactions with biopolymers.
source: It has been demonstrated previously that PEG-coated particles have little or no chemical interactions with biopolymers (Valentine et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2008), so using PEG-coated particles allows us to isolate and investigate only the interactions dominated by physical effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous published work.

claim: Both bacteria and particles aggregate in the gut.
source: It has been observed that both bacteria (Levinson et al., 2015; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Endt et al., 2010; Moor et al., 2017; Donaldson et al., 2018; Bergström et al., 2016) and particles (Maisel et al., 2015a; Ensign et al., 2012; Tirosh and Rubinstein, 1998; Maisel et al., 2015b) aggregate in the gut.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Carboxylate-coated nanoparticles are mucoadhesive.
source: Experiments have been performed in which mice are orally co-administered carboxylate-coated nanoparticles, which are mucoadhesive, and PEG-coated nanoparticles, which are mucus-penetrating (Maisel et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: PEG-coated nanoparticles are mucus-penetrating.
source: Experiments have been performed in which mice are orally co-administered carboxylate-coated nanoparticles, which are mucoadhesive, and PEG-coated nanoparticles, which are mucus-penetrating (Maisel et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Carboxylate-coated particles formed large aggregates in the center of the gut lumen.
source: The carboxylate-coated particles formed large aggregates in the center of the gut lumen.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work describing experimental observations.

claim: PEG-coated particles were sometimes found co-localized with carboxylate-coated particles and also penetrated mucus, distributing across the underlying epithelium of the SI as aggregates and single particles.
source: In contrast, PEG-coated particles were sometimes found co-localized with carboxylate-coated particles and also penetrated mucus, distributing across the underlying epithelium of the SI as aggregates and single particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published work describing experimental observations.

claim: 1-µm-diameter particles are similar in size to bacteria.
source: We chose 1-µm-diameter particles because of their similarity in size to bacteria.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about bacterial sizes.

claim: PEG-coated particles aggregate with each other and co-aggregate with digesta in the murine small intestine after oral administration.
source: We collected luminal contents after 3 hr and confirmed using confocal fluorescence and reflectance microscopy that these particles aggregated with each other and co-aggregated with what appeared to be digesta (Figure 1C and D; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Orally administered PEG-coated particles transit the SI after 3 hr.
source: On separate mice, fluorescent scanning was used to verify that particles do transit the SI after 3 hr (Figure 1A and B; Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescent scanner images shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: PEG 5 kDa coating followed by PEG 1 kDa backfilling achieves a lower zeta potential than a single coat of PEG 5 kDa.
source: We found that by coating with PEG 5 kDa and then coating again with PEG 1 kDa to backfill the remaining surface sites on the particle allowed us to achieve a lower zeta potential than applying a single coat of PEG 5 kDa (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by zeta potential measurements presented in Table 1.

claim: A near-zero zeta potential minimizes the interactions particles have in biological environments.
source: It has been suggested in the literature that a near-zero zeta potential minimizes the interactions particles have in biological environments (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Aggregates of PEG-coated particles form in SI luminal fluid in 5–10 min.
source: We found that, despite the PEG coating and low-volume fraction, aggregates of particles formed in 5–10 min (Figure 2A–D), a timescale much shorter than the transit time for food through the SI, which can be as short as ~80 min in healthy humans (Hasler et al., 2009) and ~60 min in mice (Padmanabhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-D and citations about transit times.

claim: Transit time for food through the SI can be as short as ~80 min in healthy humans.
source: We found that, despite the PEG coating and low-volume fraction, aggregates of particles formed in 5–10 min (Figure 2A–D), a timescale much shorter than the transit time for food through the SI, which can be as short as ~80 min in healthy humans (Hasler et al., 2009) and ~60 min in mice (Padmanabhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Transit time for food through the SI can be as short as ~60 min in mice.
source: We found that, despite the PEG coating and low-volume fraction, aggregates of particles formed in 5–10 min (Figure 2A–D), a timescale much shorter than the transit time for food through the SI, which can be as short as ~80 min in healthy humans (Hasler et al., 2009) and ~60 min in mice (Padmanabhan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Polymers are present in SI luminal fluid.
source: Chromatography confirmed that polymers were indeed present in the SI fluid (Figure 3A and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gel permeation chromatography data shown in Figure 3A and D.

claim: The SI is abundant in polymers with a range of MWs.
source: The estimates suggest that the SI is abundant in polymers with a range of MWs.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of GPC data and estimates of polymer properties.

claim: Less aggregation is observed in fractionated samples compared with 30- and 0.45 µm filtered samples.
source: We generally found less aggregation in the fractionated samples compared with the 30- and 0.45 µm filtered samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing aggregation in samples with different filtration treatments.

claim: When the MWCO was decreased to 3 kDa, the observed aggregation in the eluent matched the extent of aggregation observed for particles in HBSS.
source: When the MWCO was decreased to 3 kDa, the observed aggregation in the eluent matched the extent of aggregation observed for particles in HBSS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MWCO filtration experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Biopolymers in the SI are involved in the aggregation of PEG-coated particles.
source: Overall, these data supported our hypothesis that polymers were involved in the aggregation of these particles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MWCO filtration experiments.

claim: Samples from WT mice fed autoclaved diet had a lower average concentration of polymers compared with WT mice fed normal chow diet.
source: We postulate that this increase in viscosity was due to the formation of self-associating polymeric structures, although we did not test this assumption. We attribute this decrease in aggregation in the 30 µm filtered samples to slower aggregation kinetics due to decreased diffusivity of particles in this viscous medium. This decrease in aggregation at high polymer concentrations or viscosities is also observed in solutions of model polymers, as discussed in the next section.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of data from Tables 1-4 showing polymer concentrations in different experimental groups.

claim: Samples from WT mice fed autoclaved diet had polymers of lower overall MW compared with WT mice fed normal chow diet.
source: When samples from the WT mice in the MUC2KO experiments are compared with samples from the WT mice in the Rag1KO experiments are compared, it is apparent that, compared with WT mice fed the normal chow diet, samples from WT mice fed the autoclaved diet had (i) a lower average concentration of polymers and (ii) polymers of lower overall MW (see 'WT' samples in Tables 1–4).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of data from Tables 1-4 showing polymer properties in different experimental groups.

claim: The aggregation of colloids and bacteria can be controlled by altering the concentration and size of non-adsorbing polymers.
source: It has been demonstrated that the aggregation of colloids and bacteria can be controlled by altering the concentration and size of the non-adsorbing polymers to which particles are exposed (Asakura and Oosawa, 1954; Asakura and Oosawa, 1958; Vrij, 1976; Gast et al., 1983; Prasad, 2002; Lu et al., 2006; Ilett et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Particles aggregate due to depletion interactions in controlled settings with non-adsorbing polymers.
source: In these controlled settings, particles aggregate due to what are known as depletion interactions (Asakura and Oosawa, 1954; Asakura and Oosawa, 1958; Vrij, 1976).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational literature on depletion interactions.

claim: Pectin at low and very high mass concentrations shows little aggregation, while showing the most aggregation at intermediate concentrations.
source: Pectin at low (~0.05 to ~1 mg/mL) and very high mass concentrations showed little aggregation (~7 mg/mL) and showed the most aggregation at an intermediate concentration (~1.5 to ~3 mg/mL).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Fibersol-2 did not induce much aggregation up to a mass concentration of ~240 mg/mL.
source: Fibersol-2 did not induce much aggregation up to a mass concentration of ~240 mg/mL.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: More aggregation is observed in pectin-fed mice compared with Fibersol-2 fed mice in the upper SI.
source: In the 30-µm-filtered samples from the upper SI we observed more aggregation in the pectin-fed mice compared with the Fibersol-2 fed mice (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Pectin can form a gel in certain contexts.
source: This gelation is not too surprising considering that pectin can form a gel in certain contexts (Thakur et al., 1997; Saha and Bhattacharya, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pectin-fed mice have more high-MW polymers than Fibersol-2-fed mice.
source: Overall, the data from GPC suggests that the pectin-fed mice have more high-MW polymers than the Fibersol-2-fed mice.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of GPC data shown in Figure 7C and D and Tables 7 and 8.

claim: Low-MW polymers appear to be more abundant in Fibersol-2 fed mice compared with pectin-fed mice.
source: Low-MW polymers appear to be more abundant in Fibersol-2 fed mice compared with pectin-fed mice.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of GPC data shown in Figure 7C and D and Tables 7 and 8.

claim: Polymers in the diet can be used to control the aggregation of PEG-coated particles.
source: These data taken together lead us to conclude that polymers in the diet can be used to control the aggregation of PEG-coated particles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dietary fiber feeding experiments.

claim: Feeding higher MW polymers at the same mass concentration as lower MW polymers leads to an enhancement in aggregation.
source: This data further suggests that feeding higher MW polymers at the same mass concentration as lower MW polymers leads to an enhancement in aggregation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing pectin and Fibersol-2 feeding experiments.

claim: The aggregation behavior in SI luminal fluid from mice fed dietary polymers of different sizes is qualitatively consistent with aggregation behavior in simple PEG solutions driven by depletion interactions.
source: We can, however, note that visually the behavior is qualitatively consistent with the depletion-type interactions found in simple PEG solutions in Figure 4.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of experimental results with model polymer systems.

claim: PEG-coated particles form aggregates in the luminal fluid of the SI.
source: This work shows that even PEG-coated particles, which have minimal biochemical interactions, form aggregates in the luminal fluid of the SI.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main experimental finding.

claim: Dietary polymers can impact and be used to control the structure of particles in the SI.
source: It reveals a previously unknown way in which dietary polymers can impact, and be used to control, the structure of particles in the SI.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dietary fiber experiments.

claim: MUC2 may play a role in the aggregation of PEG-coated particles, but is not required for aggregation to occur.
source: We found differences in the aggregation threshold in the samples from MUC2KO and WT mice (Figure 5C–D), suggesting that although MUC2 is not required for aggregation to occur, it could play a role in the aggregation of PEG-coated particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing MUC2KO and WT mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: Immunoglobulins may play a role in aggregation, but are not required for aggregation to occur.
source: We found differences in the amount of aggregation between the Rag1KO and WT samples at different dilutions, suggesting that although immunoglobulins are not required for aggregation to occur, they could play a role in the aggregation of PEG-coated particles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing Rag1KO and WT mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mucins can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
source: It is well known that host-secreted polymers can cause aggregation of particles via chemical interactions; for example, mucins (Puri et al., 2015; Laux et al., 1986; Sajjan and Forstner, 1990; Wanke et al., 1990; Sun et al., 2007), immunoglobulins (Doe, 1989; Peterson et al., 2007; Levinson et al., 2015; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Endt et al., 2010; Bunker et al., 2017; Moor et al., 2017; Mantis et al., 2011; Donaldson et al., 2018), and proteins (Bergström et al., 2016) can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Immunoglobulins can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
source: It is well known that host-secreted polymers can cause aggregation of particles via chemical interactions; for example, mucins (Puri et al., 2015; Laux et al., 1986; Sajjan and Forstner, 1990; Wanke et al., 1990; Sun et al., 2007), immunoglobulins (Doe, 1989; Peterson et al., 2007; Levinson et al., 2015; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Endt et al., 2010; Bunker et al., 2017; Moor et al., 2017; Mantis et al., 2011; Donaldson et al., 2018), and proteins (Bergström et al., 2016) can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Proteins can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
source: It is well known that host-secreted polymers can cause aggregation of particles via chemical interactions; for example, mucins (Puri et al., 2015; Laux et al., 1986; Sajjan and Forstner, 1990; Wanke et al., 1990; Sun et al., 2007), immunoglobulins (Doe, 1989; Peterson et al., 2007; Levinson et al., 2015; Hendrickx et al., 2015; Endt et al., 2010; Bunker et al., 2017; Moor et al., 2017; Mantis et al., 2011; Donaldson et al., 2018), and proteins (Bergström et al., 2016) can cause bacteria to aggregate via an agglutination mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Non-adsorbing polymers can cause aggregation via purely physical interactions that are dependent on the physical properties of the polymers, such as their molecular weight and concentration.
source: However, non-adsorbing polymers can also cause aggregation via purely physical interactions that are dependent on the physical properties of the polymers, such as their molecular weight (MW) and concentration (Asakura and Oosawa, 1954; Asakura and Oosawa, 1958; Vrij, 1976; Gast et al., 1983; Prasad, 2002; Lu et al., 2006; Ilett et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature on depletion interactions.

claim: Current dietary guidelines do not differentiate between fibers of low and high MW.
source: We note that current dietary guidelines do not differentiate between fibers of low and high MW (USDA, 2007; USDA, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to USDA dietary guidelines.

claim: The MW of fiber is important in defining the physicochemical environment of the gut.
source: Our work implies that the MW of fiber, and the subsequent degradation of a high-MW fiber into a low-MW component (Datta et al., 2016), which we have discussed previously in the context of mucus compression, is important in defining the physicochemical environment of the gut.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and cited previous work.

claim: IgA is abundant in the SI.
source: According to the literature, IgA is abundant in the SI (Murphy et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: A signal for IgA was detected in the upper and lower SI of WT mice.
source: As expected, we saw a signal for IgA in the upper and lower SI of WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: IgG and IgM were not detected in the luminal contents of either WT or KO mice.
source: We also tested for less abundant immunoglobulins such as IgG and IgM (Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2, respectively), but did not detect their presence in the luminal contents of either WT or KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6 supplements.

claim: Neither pectin nor Fibersol-2 should be broken down in the SI.
source: According to the literature, neither of these two polymers should be broken down in the SI (Fibersol, 2018; Holloway et al., 1983; Coenen et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MUC2 is the primary mucin secreted in the SI.
source: It has been demonstrated that mucins can aggregate and bind to bacteria in vitro (Puri et al., 2015; Laux et al., 1986; Sajjan and Forstner, 1990; Wanke et al., 1990; Sun et al., 2007); thus, we wanted to test whether mucins, such as Mucin 2 (MUC2), which is the primary mucin secreted in the SI (Ermund et al., 2013; Johansson et al., 2011), drive the aggregation of PEG-coated particles in SI fluid.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Western blot did not detect MUC2 in the SI of either WT or MUC2KO mice.
source: The Western blot detected MUC2 in the colons of WT mice and not MUC2KO mice, as expected, however it did not detect a signal for MUC2 in the SI of either the WT or MUC2KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The lack of MUC2 signal in the SI of WT mice may be due to low levels of MUC2 present in the luminal contents of the SI.
source: We speculate that the lack of MUC2 signal in the SI of WT mice may be due to low levels of MUC2 present in the luminal contents of the SI.
evidence: This is speculation based on the Western blot results.

claim: The upper small intestine luminal fluid has a pH of 6.0 ± 0.1.
source: We found that the upper small intestine (USI) luminal fluid was pH = 6.0 ± 0.1 and for the lower small intestine (LSI) pH = 7.5 ± 0.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lower small intestine luminal fluid has a pH of 7.5 ± 0.3.
source: We found that the upper small intestine (USI) luminal fluid was pH = 6.0 ± 0.1 and for the lower small intestine (LSI) pH = 7.5 ± 0.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: HBSS has a pH of 7.6 ± 0.1.
source: For the HBSS used, pH = 7.6 ± 0.1 (See Materials and methods), which matches that of the LSI but not the USI.
evidence: This claim is supported by pH measurements described in Materials and methods.

claim: At high ionic strengths (~170 mM), electrostatic repulsions between particles are screened to length scales on the order of the Debye screening length ~0.7 nm.
source: At the high ionic strengths of these buffered aqueous solutions (~170 mM), any electrostatic repulsions that can occur between particles should be screened to length scales on the order of the Debye screening length ~0.7 nm (Yethiraj and van Blaaderen, 2003; Jones, 2002), nearly an order of magnitude smaller than the estimated length of the surface PEG brush (~6.4 nm; see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This claim is based on established theory cited from published literature and calculations.

claim: The estimated length of the surface PEG brush is ~6.4 nm.
source: At the high ionic strengths of these buffered aqueous solutions (~170 mM), any electrostatic repulsions that can occur between particles should be screened to length scales on the order of the Debye screening length ~0.7 nm (Yethiraj and van Blaaderen, 2003; Jones, 2002), nearly an order of magnitude smaller than the estimated length of the surface PEG brush (~6.4 nm; see Materials and methods for more details).
evidence: This is calculated in the Materials and methods section using the Alexander-de Gennes approximation.

claim: Mucins and immunoglobulins are polymers that can self-associate into structures of very high MW.
source: We note that mucins and immunoglobulins are polymers that can also self-associate into structures of very high MW (Ambort et al., 2012; Grey et al., 1971; Kerr, 1990), suggesting that they could cause aggregation via both physical and chemical mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mucins and immunoglobulins could cause aggregation via both physical and chemical mechanisms.
source: We note that mucins and immunoglobulins are polymers that can also self-associate into structures of very high MW (Ambort et al., 2012; Grey et al., 1971; Kerr, 1990), suggesting that they could cause aggregation via both physical and chemical mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation based on the properties of mucins and immunoglobulins and the experimental findings.

claim: A study published during review of this manuscript showed in vitro work with model buffer solutions of mucins, DNA, and other biopolymers implying that aggregation of bacteria by host-polymers can be depletion-mediated.
source: Interestingly, during the review of this manuscript, a study was published with in vitro work done using model buffer solutions of mucins, DNA, and other biopolymers further implying that aggregation of bacteria by host-polymers can be depletion-mediated (Secor et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recently published study.

claim: Flow in non-Newtonian fluids can induce particle aggregation.
source: In vivo, it will also be important to consider the effects of flow, as it has been shown that flow in non-Newtonian fluids can induce particle aggregation (Highgate, 1966; Michele et al., 1977; Kim and Helgeson, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The combination of flow and polymer elasticity can lead to aggregation.
source: In particular, studies have suggested that the combination of flow and polymer elasticity can lead to aggregation (Highgate and Whorlow, 1970) and that shear thinning viscosity can influence aggregation as well (Snijkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Shear thinning viscosity can influence aggregation.
source: In particular, studies have suggested that the combination of flow and polymer elasticity can lead to aggregation (Highgate and Whorlow, 1970) and that shear thinning viscosity can influence aggregation as well (Snijkers et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Bacteria in the healthy SI are found at low-volume fractions similar to the volume fraction used in the experiments (~0.001).
source: A low-volume fraction was chosen because bacteria in the healthy SI are found at similarly low-volume fractions (Rubio-Tapia et al., 2009; O'Hara and Shanahan, 2006; Simon and Gorbach, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.
